Tournament and match context loading for score updates

runs.comparability_note: Same seeded workload, different tournament progress (35 finished initially versus 24 previously); fewer occupied courts after idle and more check-ins. Live before/after differences are observational, not isolated performance measurements.
findings: All 1077 client score updates were logged successfully by the server and matched on TV. No check-in errors.
Typical score total fell from 12.4 to 6.9 ms; p95 increased from 63.6 to 108.2 ms. Different tournament progress prevents isolated attribution.
16 replans across 6 integrations, with up to 6 attempts; sampled conflicts predominantly local network score/press history. No tournament lock in any observed plan.

No planner early unchanged skip logged in this run. Two no-change integrations inside the client window still performed full planning (245 and 265 ms). Fetch sync_skipped alone does not imply early planner bypass.

Long context reads include the already projected tournament read (up to 531.1 ms), suggesting executor/event-loop contention; other display and umpire refresh paths still fetch the full tournament document.
Logged display court fan-out phases reached 927.1 ms. Only phases above the 100 ms threshold are present, so this is not their full distribution.

Automatic compactions for 13 collections occupied approximately 594.515 to 595.088 seconds of the client run (individual durations 409 to 539 ms); no logged score-update processing interval overlapped this window. They do not explain this run's worst score outliers.
Post-sync auto-call planned 16 times, applied no record changes, and held its locks an estimated median 1 ms (previously 11 ms). Total planner time still had a 254.5 ms median.

runs.source_scope: Client ten-minute window. Score timestamps are exact client trace_id send times. Compactions use exact timestamps and approximate score processing intervals.
runs.comparability_note: Same seeded workload but later tournament progress: 49 finished initially versus 35 previously. Current run kept approximately 13 occupied courts including after idle, previously approximately 10 after idle. Results reflect the combined point-rebase, projection, canonical-object and assignment-index changes and different tournament progress, not an isolated measurement of any one change.
findings: All 1195 score updates were processed successfully and matched on TV; 48 check-in requests had no reported errors.
Server score median 4.3 ms and p95 48.8 ms, previously 6.9 and 108.2 ms. TV weighted mean 44.9 ms, previously 55.7 ms.
One required replan changed btp_needsync and setup.state (match end), compared with 16 replans previously. Four concurrent point states were rebased across two integrations.
Three early unchanged planner skips in the idle phase took 14, 62 and 11 ms. One earlier no-change full plan still took 267 ms.
Median completed integration 432 ms, previously 680 ms. Estimated median held time 77.5 ms, previously 73 ms: lock hold did not improve at the median.

All match integrations inspected 519 matches; median 505 bypassed crafting by signature. Signature work median 21 ms, dependency lookup 10 ms, hidden-bye scan 13 ms; these remain repeated work for small deltas. craft_ms sums potentially overlapping asynchronous durations and must not be interpreted as independent CPU time.
Fifteen post-sync auto-call plans made no record changes; median total time 80 ms and estimated median held time 1 ms.

Largest server score latencies 753.4 and 484 ms overlapped simultaneous automatic compactions at 594.6-595.1 seconds. Temporal overlap supports compaction as a contributor but is not an isolated causal measurement.
Multiple simultaneous projected context reads still exceeded 200 ms, including validation during an integration; shared executor or event-loop contention remains to be isolated.
Verbose tablet-loop debug output produced 48601 entries across the server log. A timing-only follow-up run can separate instrumentation cost from application work.

runs.source_scope: Client ten-minute window only. Score times use exact client send timestamps encoded in trace_id; other phases use the nearest debug timestamp by log-line distance. Lock-held values are residual estimates from total minus final plan and wait, include publication/scheduling and may include previous failed planning attempts; not direct measurements of lock acquisition/release. Compactions use exact logged timestamps.
runs.comparability_note: Same seeded ten-minute workload, later tournament progress: 60 finished games initially versus 49 previously; 13 versus 11 finish confirmations and 56 versus 48 check-in requests. Live before/after differences are observational and do not isolate the selector change.
findings: All 1192 score updates (1179 points and 13 finish confirmations) succeeded and matched on TV. 56 check-in requests had no reported errors.

Actual integrated matches fell from 519 per pass to median 72, range 3-216, across 21 planning passes. The new selected count additionally includes 519 incoming BTP records rejected by existing IsMatch/ReverseHomeAway integration guards; these have no local match document and are repeatedly selected. It must not be compared directly to 519 stored games.

Selection cost median 26 ms; signature computation median 15 ms versus 21 previously. Dependency cache reused on only 3 of 21 passes, with cached lookup 2 ms and hidden-bye scan 0. Median full match loop remained 39 ms.

Full incremental integration median increased from 432 to 514 ms, mean from 554.6 to 819.6 ms. Estimated held median 77.5 to 80 ms. Writes/planned changes increased: median 23 versus 8.5 records and 72 versus 37.5 match locks. No tournament lock was acquired.

Five replans versus one previously; two cycles required three planning attempts. Logged reasons include successor preparation, pending BTP result, ordinary point state and player check-ins/court assignment. Some point-only mismatches are still rejected even though six point states were rebased across five passes; the validation rules require further inspection before attributing these cases to a bug.

Post-sync auto-call produced zero record changes across all 14 plans yet median total duration increased from 80 to 395 ms. This is a separate measurable source of repeated work and executor/event-loop contention.
Score median remained 4.3 ms, p95 increased 48.8 to 61.1 ms, max fell 753.4 to 482.9 ms. Weighted TV mean increased 44.9 to 47.3 ms. This does not demonstrate an overall performance gain.

Largest score delays did not overlap automatic compactions. At 173 seconds finish cleanup took 407.2 ms and subsequent score requests waited up to 432.1 ms. At 583 seconds context loading took 208.9 ms and match update 270.1 ms. These timings locate the blocking phases but do not isolate their cause.

Automatic compactions near 588 seconds overlapped the worst post-auto-call duration (887 ms), not the largest point update. Full-log tablet-loop entries numbered 48659; the verbose diagnostics remain enabled as in the previous comparison.

Load phase averaged 11.9 occupied courts. Several changes were combined (auto-call precheck, match selection filter, indexed finish cleanup, normalization fingerprints). Differences do not isolate a single change.
findings: Completed ten-minute benchmark: all 1178 score updates (1166 points, 12 finish confirmations) succeeded and matched on TV; 40 check-in requests had zero reported errors.

Score total mean improved from 16.9 to 10.0 ms and p95 from 61.1 to 29.0 ms. Median increased from 4.3 to 5.0 ms; maximum increased from 482.9 to 717.1 ms. Queue p95 decreased from 2.3 to 0.3 ms, maximum from 432.1 to 78.2 ms.
Weighted tablet-to-TV mean improved from 47.3 to 18.1 ms. Per-phase TV medians were 9 ms in all active phases. Client report phase summaries cannot reconstruct an exact overall TV percentile.

Normalization fingerprints were checked 16 times: median 1 ms, maximum 3 ms; three unchanged snapshots skipped normalizers and snapshot loading, including two during active scoring after idle. Remaining thirteen passes loaded normalization state (median 10 ms). Full normalization phase median 23.5 ms versus 33 ms previously; relevant changes still trigger complete normalization work.

Auto-call precheck skipped five of twelve attempts because courts were occupied. Seven remaining plans still wrote zero records and cost median 123 ms versus 395 ms across fourteen plans previously. Their inputs changed, so this does not establish a precheck cache bug.

Match selection now excludes all 519 non-integrated source records before selecting among the 519 integrated games. Sixteen passes processed median 93 games, maximum 187; prior median was 72 actual games. Dependency cache hit only three passes. Filtering works but this run does not show lower selection CPU cost (delta median 29 ms versus 26 ms, match loop 41.5 versus 39 ms). Hidden-bye handling remains represented in logged scan phases; the workload does not establish end-to-end coverage of every bye path.

Fifteen BTP integrations completed, one replan versus five previously. Total median 497 ms versus 514 ms, mean 517.1 versus 819.6 ms, max 1594 versus 3359 ms. Actual apply median increased from 73.5 to 95 ms; held residual median increased from 80 to 96 ms. There were no tournament-lock plans. These numbers do not demonstrate shorter typical lock holding.

All twelve finish updates took median 62 ms, maximum 118 ms. Only one aggregate finish-cleanup phase exceeded the 100 ms logging threshold (113.8 ms), versus a previously observed 407.2 ms slow cleanup. No cleanup subphase exceeded the threshold; missing logs do not imply zero time.

Worst score update at elapsed 595375 ms took 717.1 ms, including 628.8 ms loading context and only 1.8 ms queue wait. Logged collection compactions overlap these reads; matches compaction lasted 676.4 ms. Six other context-load delays ranged from 227.4 to 264.1 ms without compaction overlap. Their root cause is not isolated by these logs. Context match/tournament/court reads are parallel and their durations must not be added.

Several changes were combined and the tournament began at 73 finished games versus 60; check-ins and average occupied load-phase courts also differ. Improvement cannot be attributed solely to fingerprint caching.

findings: Completed ten-minute benchmark: 1164 points and 17 finishes yielded 1181 successful score updates, all matched on TV; 48 check-in requests had no reported errors. Four preparation check-ins were pending at the two-minute window boundary; the report does not establish their later individual completion times.

Server score mean improved from 10.0 to 8.5 ms, median from 5.0 to 4.4 ms, p95 from 29.0 to 27.4 ms, maximum from 717.1 to 314.6 ms. Lock/resource-queue p95 remained 0.3 ms; maximum decreased from 78.2 to 68.1 ms. Weighted tablet-to-TV mean improved slightly from 18.1 to 17.2 ms.

Thirteen automatic compactions completed without overlapping, with durations 54.0-192.2 ms versus the previous simultaneous group at 431.2-676.4 ms. Match compaction took 192.2 versus 676.4 ms. Startup compactions still overlap but precede the client window. The new automatic schedule was exercised over the full benchmark, not merely deferred beyond its end.

One score update at elapsed 180951 ms overlapped the match compaction: total 173.1 ms, context match wait 148.6 ms, read 0.1 ms. Only its match read exceeded the 100ms threshold and compaction_pending_at_enqueue was true. A single compaction still blocks its own datastore executor.

Four other slow context loads took 216.2-254.6 ms without any compaction overlap. All three context reads were delayed together; actual match reads took 0.1-0.3 ms and tournament/court reads rounded to 0.0 ms. Reported queue depth was zero but excludes the active executor task. First event-loop turn took 0.1-2.2 ms, so these measurements neither establish an initial event-loop stall nor exclude later CPU/callback delays or in-flight datastore tasks. The remaining delay occurs before executing the read, not during object lookup/copy.

Worst server score update took 314.6 ms, including device_info 311.8 ms. The concurrent panel-group refresh lasted 312.4 ms; these phases overlap and must not be added. Device info includes hostname resolution and display settings reads/updates; logs do not isolate which operation caused the delay.

Seventeen finish updates had median 52.7 ms and maximum 113.2 ms versus median 62.0 and maximum 118.0 ms across twelve finishes previously. No aggregate finish-cleanup phase crossed the 100ms threshold.

Sixteen BTP integrations completed with one replan and no tournament-lock plans. Total median 520.5 ms versus 497 ms; mean 503.0 versus 517.1 ms; max 938 versus 1594 ms. Actual apply median remained 95 ms; residual held estimate median 97.5 versus 96 ms. This change does not demonstrate shorter typical sync locking.

Auto-call precheck skipped eleven of thirteen attempts because courts were occupied; two remaining plans still wrote zero records and cost 175 and 291 ms. Different occupancy prevents attributing fewer plans to a code change in this run.

Normalization hash checks had median 1 ms and two unchanged passes skipped processing. Later tournament progress and different court occupancy/check-in/finish counts limit before-after comparability. Neither runtime changes nor compaction improvements alone isolate the contribution of each optimization.

findings: All 1135 score updates (1124 points and 11 finish confirmations) succeeded and matched on TV. 56 player check-in requests had zero reported errors; no pending preparation-player check-ins remained at the two-minute checkpoint.

Score total median 4.9 ms, mean 10.2 ms, p95 36.4 ms and max 385.9 ms versus 4.4/8.5/27.4/314.6 ms in the preceding run. Weighted tablet-to-TV mean 22.5 ms versus 17.2 ms. Added diagnostics and changed tournament progress prevent attributing these differences to one cause; this step did not implement a speed optimization.

Four threshold-logged context waits took 205.0-241.6 ms. Actual individual canonical-object lookup/copy times were 0.0-0.2 ms. Timer lateness 184.3-219.4 ms confirms delayed event-loop scheduling after a quick first turn (0.2-2.9 ms), rather than expensive object lookup. No automatic compaction overlapped these four slow points.

For three of these waits all three context reads were logged: previous find/findOne tasks finished their callbacks about 185.1-221.5 ms before the next read began, while preceding task runtimes were only 17.4-22.8 ms. The fourth logged only the tournament read and similarly showed 200.4 ms since its previous callback returned. These samples expose delayed executor release/start scheduling, not a long synchronous user callback or pending persistence.

Three slow device-info parents took 252.3/286.7/377.7 ms. Settings reads accounted for 251.6/286.2/377.1 ms, cached hostname resolution was 0.0 ms and notifications 0.2-0.4 ms. At the worst point, tournament findOne and device-settings findOne both took about 376 ms with no persistence, completing beside BTP response_received. BTP decoding uses synchronous decompression/XML parsing and is a plausible event-loop blocker, but its CPU time was not directly measured in this live run. Moving device-info work alone cannot remove an event-loop stall.

Repeated slow context waits coincide with automatic preparation selection results. Read-only offline reconstruction of the persisted 519-game tournament after the run reproduced 168.8-183.1 ms of synchronous preparation-selection computation (mean 174.8, median 175.1) with zero selected matches. Instrumenting one calculation counted 831 frontier-block-position rebuilds, 417847 match visits and 1662 position lookups. CPU sampling attributed 407 of 890.2 ms (45.7 percent) across five calculations to building those positions including descendant work. This proves repeated CPU work in that algorithm; the later snapshot and separate process do not establish the cause of every live stall.

Recommended next individual proposal: create a small per-calculation frontier-position index using canonical object identity and ID fallback, build once per exact ordered match list, then reuse for candidate eligibility and diagnostics. Preserve separate lists, original ordering, block semantics, first-match fallback, missing-match infinity and bye behavior. No cross-calculation cache or live implementation authorized yet.

Seventeen BTP integrations had median total 535 ms versus 520.5 ms previously, median apply 116 ms versus 95 ms. No tournament lock plans. Maximum total 5131 ms was the initial cycle, starting about 1.9 seconds before the client and completing 3.2 seconds into it, with two retries during startup/check-ins. The sixteen later cycles had mean 487.5, median 527.5 and max 995 ms. Final-plan duration is cumulative from cycle start; subtracting it and final lock wait yields a residual around final commit, not the sum of all lock-held intervals.

Four replans: two in the startup cycle, one preparation-successor flag change and one score-state mismatch. Three whole-sync skips took median 22 ms; two normalization computations skipped with fingerprint check median 1 ms. Eight auto-call prechecks skipped because no courts were free. Seven post-auto-call plans still produced no record changes (median 145 ms).

Thirteen automatic compactions were sequential with no overlap, 50.9-207.7 ms. All twelve worst score updates had no automatic-compaction overlap. Spreading compactions continues to work, but does not explain the remaining largest score delays.

findings: All 1138 score updates (1126 points and 12 finish confirmations) succeeded and matched on TV. 28 player check-in requests had no reported errors; no preparation-player check-ins were pending at the two-minute checkpoint.

Score total median 4.6 ms versus 4.9, mean 8.3 versus 10.2, p95 25.2 versus 36.4 and max 196.9 versus 385.9 in the diagnostics baseline. Weighted tablet-to-TV mean 17.7 versus 22.5 ms. This is consistent with reduced preparation-selection CPU work, but the different tournament state and 28 versus 56 check-ins prevent attributing the entire live difference to this change.

Threshold-logged context outliers fell from four at 205-242 ms to two at 117.4/122.3 ms. One at 226.9 seconds waited 122 ms behind tournament compaction; persistence was active when queued and its callback had returned only 0.3 ms before the read. Timer lateness was just 0.3 ms, separating this genuine per-collection queue wait from an event-loop stall.

The other context outlier at 277.4 seconds had first-turn delay 114.6 ms and timer lateness 94.9 ms; match executor was idle at enqueue, object lookup/copy 0.1 ms, and no automatic compaction overlapped it. It occurred during replanning of a BTP sync, near incremental_refresh (179 ms). Its exact synchronous CPU source was not profiled in this live run.

Only one device-info parent exceeded 100 ms, at 147.2 versus three up to 377.7 ms previously. Settings read 146.6 ms, hostname 0 ms, notify 0.3 ms. Its DB findOne task took 116.4 ms without persistence, beside the delayed context read during sync replanning. These waits overlap other asynchronous phases and must not be added together.

Largest point total 196.9 ms at 91 seconds consists of queue wait 165.2 ms and processing 31.7 ms. The concurrent sync planned 98 changed records and 237 match locks including this match and court, with final apply 154 ms. Shared-resource contention is consistent with the evidence; this is not evidence of a global tournament lock. No tournament lock was planned in any completed cycle.

Seventeen BTP integrations: total median 520 ms versus 535, final apply median 99 versus 116. Excluding the previous startup cycle, previous total mean was 487.5 ms versus 575.8 now; whole-sync speed therefore did not improve consistently. Maximum 2144 ms needed three planning attempts because preparation-successor flags changed twice. Final integration apply was 185 ms; the 2.1-second cycle was not one continuous lock hold.

Three replans in total: one score-state mismatch and two preparation-successor flag mismatches. Two whole-sync skips (22/74 ms), four normalization skips and nine auto-call precheck skips for no free courts. Fingerprint check median 1 ms. Five post-auto-call plans still made zero record changes (median 199 ms).

Twelve finish confirmations had median total 57 ms versus 67.5 previously and max 128.1 ms versus 132.4. One finish_cleanup aggregate was logged at 123.6 ms, overlapping direct tablet refresh at 112.6 ms. No evidence here supports restarting a full-match cleanup scan.

Thirteen automatic compactions remained sequential, 59.6-184.5 ms, with no errors. Tournament compaction accounts for two of the twelve worst point overlaps. Match compaction 184.5 ms did not overlap the worst point.

Proposed next item, not yet approved: investigate and narrow sync lock expansion by changed field/dependency type. resources() currently expands participant/court relations for any setup difference or match result/end change; this may include metadata-only changes. Count provenance before removing expansion, keep direct write locks and required participant/official/court dependencies, validate concurrent scores, finishes, check-ins and byes.

findings: All 1194 score updates (1180 points, 14 confirmed finishes) succeeded and matched on TV. 34 player check-in requests had no reported errors; none pending at the two-minute checkpoint.

Completed sync plans have median 51 match locks versus 135 previously, max 211 versus 237. Three nonempty plans (15, 2, 2 match writes) needed no relation expansion. Other participant/court/result dependencies still expand. Changes also fell from median 24 to 15, so the lock-count difference is not an isolated measurement of the classifier.

No overall live latency improvement: score median 4.4 versus 4.6 ms, mean 11.5 versus 8.3, p95 54.2 versus 25.2, max 368.3 versus 196.9. Weighted tablet-to-TV mean 24.0 versus 17.7 ms. Current tournament has 124 versus 112 initially finished games, 34 versus 28 check-ins and higher occupied-court load.

Largest score queue wait 116.1 versus 165.2 ms previously, but queue p95 1.9 versus 0.6 and mean 1.0 versus 0.5 ms. At 158 seconds this point shares its match/court with a sync whose final plan locks 202 matches for 49 record changes, including 25 participant and eight state changes; final apply 109 ms. No tournament lock planned. Shared resources are consistent with contention, not direct proof of one particular holder.

Worst point at 219.8 seconds took 368.3 ms with only 0.1 ms resource-queue wait. Device settings read 343.2 ms and court-group panel refresh 344.3 ms overlap. Two independent findOne tasks took 342.3/342.9 ms with no persistence, immediately beside BTP response_received. No automatic compaction overlapped. Shared process scheduling is suspected; device lookup itself is not established as the CPU cause.

Second-worst point at 62 seconds took 339.8 ms, including context wait 303.9 ms. All three context executors were idle when enqueued; first event-loop turn delayed 303.4 ms, timer lateness 283.9 ms, actual lookups/copies only 0-0.1 ms. BTP response_received is the immediately preceding log entry; no compaction overlap. BTP decode synchronously decompresses, parses XML and converts its DOM before response_received is emitted. Decoder CPU time has not yet been separately measured.

Three slow context parents: 303.9 ms common process stall, 105.8 ms court-compaction queue wait (timer lateness 0.1 ms), and 101 ms tournament executor/scheduling delay (timer lateness 48 ms). The two largest score outliers are unrelated to a long resource-lock queue wait.

Seventeen BTP integrations: total median 645 versus 520 ms, mean 729.2 versus 575.8; final apply median 69 versus 99 ms, max 239 versus 218. Five replans versus three, including court/tablet allocation changes and two point-state mismatches. Longest total 1921 ms takes three planning attempts, with final apply 69 ms; it is not one uninterrupted 1.9-second lock hold.

Three whole-sync skips, three normalization skips, fingerprint check median 1 ms, ten auto-call precheck skips for no free courts. Four post-auto-call plans still make zero changes, total median 216.5 ms, max 414. Twelve automatic compactions within client window remain sequential, with no reported errors.

Next proposed individual step, not authorized: measure BTP response decompression, UTF-8 conversion, XML parsing and DOM-to-object conversion separately, before deciding which synchronous work should move out of the Node.js request loop. The correlation at response_received is evidence for investigation, not a proven decoder bottleneck.

findings: All 1194 score updates (1179 points and 15 finish confirmations) succeeded and matched on TV. 24 check-ins had no reported errors and none pending at two minutes.

Nineteen full SENDTOURNAMENTINFO responses decoded synchronously on the main Node.js thread, taking 296.9-417.0 ms; median 319.8, mean 330.7. XML size about 2.12 MB, compressed packet about 86 KB. This directly establishes a recurrent main-thread decoder stall independent of resource locks.

Stage medians: decompression 1.8 ms, UTF-8 conversion 7.1, XML DOM parsing 262.7, DOM-to-object conversion 48.3. XML parsing accounts for 82.1 percent of summed decoder wall time. Phase medians are not additive; process CPU samples include parallel background/GC work and are not exclusive thread CPU.
All 202 SENDUPDATE replies decoded successfully, median 0.3 ms, max 1.9. Large tournament replies are the meaningful offloading target; small update acknowledgements have negligible decode cost.

Five client trace timestamps fall inside full-response decoder intervals. At 309.424 seconds a point is sent while decoding continues for another 258 ms; the server then reports only 105.3 ms total. Server timings start after handler entry and exclude earlier socket/event-loop delay. Adding server duration to client send time is not a valid way to establish a processing overlap interval.

Overall score total median 4.3 versus 4.4 ms previously, mean 8.5 versus 11.5, p95 35.2 versus 54.2 and max 174.8 versus 368.3. Weighted tablet-to-TV mean 15.0 versus 24.0 ms. This step only adds instrumentation; different tournament progress, 24 versus 34 check-ins and changed occupied courts preclude attributing improvement to these measurements.

Seventeen syncs: median total 521 versus 645 ms, final apply 88 versus 69, match locks 49 versus 51, changed records 23 versus 15. Three replans versus five: two point-state mismatches and one preparation-successor flag mismatch. No tournament locks. Extended validation median returned to 1 ms and max 5 versus 2/100; the earlier elapsed-time outlier is not evidence that the projection itself consumed 100 ms of CPU.

Largest server score delay 174.8 ms is a finish waiting 130 ms on shared resources. A nearby ordinary point waits 111.4 ms behind active match compaction; actual lookup/copy 0.2 ms. Two other slow contexts 105.2/102.9 show timer lateness 84.4/64.5 and no compaction. These do not overlap the full-response decoder timestamps; other scheduling/queue causes remain.

Three whole-sync skips, fingerprint check median 1 ms, ten auto-call precheck skips. Seven post-auto-call plans still make zero changes (median 143 ms). Thirteen automatic compactions remain sequential with no reported errors, 60.4-205.5 ms. No device-info parent exceeds the phase logging threshold in this run.

Recommended next individual proposal, not authorized: decode full tournament responses in a persistent worker thread, including decompression, UTF-8, XML parsing and object conversion. Retain small update acknowledgement decoding on the main thread. Preserve response format and existing timeout/reset/termination/validation behavior. Structured-clone transfer cost still needs measurement; total decode work does not automatically decrease.
Analysis and documentation only: no server-source edits, live tournament mutations, live workload starts or server restarts.
